[...] Enclitics and suffixes, which are all monosyllabic, form a phonological word with their host. When they attach to a multi-syllabic word, they cause the stress to shift one syllable to the right. [...] Some roots diverge from the trochaic pattern and have stress on the initial or final syllable rather than the penultimate syllable. These always contain a heavy syllable, which in Reta are syllables with either diphthongs, single long vowels such as /eː oː aː/, or geminated vowels. new_statements.rule_in_words: Default: trochaic, stress on the penultimate syllable of the (phonological) word (/ˈɓi.ɓɑ/ 'red', /ɑ.ˈgɑ.lɑ/ 'laugh'). Heavy syllables -- those with a long vowel /eː oː aː/, a diphthong, or a geminate vowel (codas do not count) -- always carry stress, so roots with a heavy final (or initial) syllable have final (or initial) stress (/tɑ.ˈlaː/ 'bone', /ɓɑ.ˈloːn/ 'enemy', /kɑ.ˈmɑus/ 'so-so'); apparent minimal pairs like /ˈtɑ.lɑ/ vs /tɑ.ˈlaː/ differ in vowel length/quality, so stress is analysed as non-phonemic and predictable from weight plus the penultimate default. Heavy syllables almost never occur before the penult within a root.
new_statements.secondary_stress: When a prefix with a long vowel (applicativizing person prefixes, Set III possessive prefixes) is added, the prefix takes the primary (initial) stress and the root's own penultimate/final stress is retained as secondary: /mɑ.ˈnaː/ 'place' > /ˈgeː.mɑ.ˌnaː/ 'her/his/its place'; /ˈpu.ni/ 'hold' > /ˈtoː.ˌpu.ni/ 'together' (p. 197-198, ex. 17). No other secondary/rhythmic stress described.
new_statements.exceptions: Non-penultimate stress only in roots containing a heavy syllable (exx. 15-16). Monosyllabic enclitics and suffixes (e.g. =mi 'in, at', denominal -i) form a phonological word with the host and shift stress one syllable to the right: [ˈbu.rɑŋ] 'sky' > [bu.ˈrɑŋ=mi] 'in the sky'; [kɑ.lɑm.ˈbɑ.hɑ] 'Kalabahi' > [kɑ.lɑm.bɑ.ˈhɑ=mi] (p. 196-197, ex. 14). Long vowels occur only in stressed syllables (p. 193).
new_statements.domain_note: Domain is the phonological word = root/stem plus monosyllabic enclitics and suffixes (stress computed over host+clitic); statements based on elicited citation forms and a c. 12k-word text corpus from Pura Selatan (Southern Pura). Author-uploaded copy read; it carries the publisher DOI and the published page numbers, so locators should match the De Gruyter print.
new_statements.identity_note: Source describes Reta (rett1240, ISO ret) as spoken in Pura Selatan (Southern Pura islet, village Retta), where the fieldwork was done; the author states there are no dialect differences within the Pura community and only small phonological/lexical differences with the Ternate-islet and Alor-coast (Wolang, Hula) settlements. Stokhof 1975 treated 'Retta' as a Blagar dialect (lists 'Blagar (Retta on Pura/Ternate)'); Willemsen, following Steinhauer 2010, treats Reta as a separate language from Blagar (blag1240).
